title: Eufy vs Arlo: Which No-Subscription Camera Is Better?
excerpt: Eufy built its cameras around local storage; Arlo built around cloud plans. How the two no-subscription approaches compare, and the fine print to check.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
Neither brand charges you to record, in the narrow sense — but they reached that point from opposite directions. Eufy is built around local storage with no required plan; Arlo is built around cloud subscriptions, with local storage bolted onto some models. Which no-subscription camera is better depends on which trade-off you can live with, so this comparison focuses on the design difference, the fine print, and a checklist for choosing.

"No subscription" does not mean the same thing at both companies. At Eufy it generally means core recording happens locally with no plan. At Arlo it often means the camera records, while the features that make footage useful — certain detection types, longer retention, cloud backup — sit behind a paid tier on many models.

The core design difference

Eufy, Anker's smart-home brand, centers its systems on local storage: hubs with built-in storage, plus microSD support on many models, so clips stay on hardware you own. Arlo's lineup historically assumes cloud — plans for storage and detection — though several Arlo models add local recording through a microSD slot or a base station that accepts a hard drive. Storage options change across each brand's range, so verify the exact model before assuming either way.

Where each one tends to fit

Eufy tends to fit

Households that want zero recurring bills, self-contained recording, and are comfortable managing their own storage, passwords, and firmware updates. Local-first systems also keep working for live view on your own network when the internet goes down, though remote access may suffer.

Arlo tends to fit

People who want a large accessory ecosystem — lights, sirens, doorbells, mounts — and a wide range of outdoor options, and who accept cloud fees as the cost of that breadth. Arlo is also known for polished apps and many camera shapes, which matters if you plan to grow the system over time.

The fine print that decides the comparison

  • Detection tiers: basic motion alerts are free on both brands; person, package, and vehicle detection often requires a plan — check the current model's support page.
  • Retention behavior: local storage loops when full; cloud plans keep clips longer. Confirm retention length on the plan page, not the box.
  • Sharing: both let families share access, but guest-sharing rules and limits differ by plan tier.
  • Ecosystem cost: accessories add up on both sides, so compare the whole system — camera, hub, and add-ons — rather than one device.

One check separates the two in daily use: unplug your internet for ten minutes and see what keeps recording. A hub with built-in storage usually keeps saving clips and shows them once the app reconnects, while a cloud-first camera may keep only a short local buffer or nothing at all until the connection returns. That single test tells you more about no-subscription life than any feature table, because break-ins and storms are exactly when connections drop.

The security history worth knowing

In 2024, security researchers disclosed a widely reported vulnerability affecting some Eufy cameras that could allow unauthorized access to live streams; Anker acknowledged the issue and issued fixes. Both brands have faced scrutiny, and any internet-connected camera carries risk. Whatever you choose: enable two-factor authentication, keep firmware updated, and use a strong, unique password.

The checklist before you choose

  1. Decide storage first — local-only, cloud, or both — then filter brands by it.
  2. Open the exact model's support page and list every feature that requires a plan.
  3. Confirm the camera records usable clips with no account tier active at all.
  4. If you already own one brand's gear, expect a second app when mixing ecosystems.
  5. Check the return policy: detection quality is the feature most likely to disappoint, and you can only judge it at your own property.

The verdict: if "no subscription" means never paying again, Eufy's local-first design gets closer to that promise out of the box. If you want a broad accessory ecosystem and treat cloud fees as a normal cost of that flexibility, Arlo fits better. Features drift between models and firmware updates, so treat any spec sheet as a snapshot and verify current details on the product page — and see how other pairings stack up in our Ring vs Arlo and Wyze vs Eufy comparisons before committing.
